solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Unfortunately Rome date not up to much

indicators.note: something that goes unfortunately goes wrong, so the letters end up in the wrong order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A disappointing romantic evening out in the Italian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rome date' looks like a holiday romance, but the eight letters are simply rearranged into MODERATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something only middling or mediocre in quality is described as fair, average, unremarkable.

indicators.note: asks how a word would be spoken, pointing to a word that is pronounced the same as another

blocks.note: insight is perception or understanding

explanation.surface: A campaign slogan urging people to raise awareness of some cause.
explanation.walkthrough: INSIGHT, a word for awareness, is pronounced exactly like INCITE.
explanation.definitionFit: To incite someone is to urge or stir them into action, a stronger synonym for spurring on.

clue.text: Foreign Office back on track? Absolutely

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: FO is the standard abbreviation for the Foreign Office
a racecourse or running track is a course

explanation.surface: A question about whether British diplomacy is going to plan, answered emphatically.
explanation.walkthrough: The Foreign Office is the British government department for diplomacy; 'on' simply places the reversed abbreviation before the track.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are emphatic ways of agreeing, meaning certainly or without any doubt, in reply to a question.

blocks.note: first meaning: to succeed in an exam or test
second meaning: to spend time idly, as in to let the hours go by

explanation.walkthrough: 'While' looks like the conjunction meaning 'during', but 'while away' is a verb phrase for spending time.
explanation.definitionFit: One verb covers succeeding in an examination and also spending hours idly, as when you kill time.

clue.text: Asked to pay but sick in bed

indicators.note: one thing lying inside another means it is enclosed by it

blocks.note: sick means unwell
taken as written

explanation.surface: An invalid confined to bed still gets sent the invoice.
explanation.walkthrough: The sickness word sits inside the bed, and the picture of a patient receiving a hospital bill disguises the split.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sent an invoice means a demand has been made for payment of money owed.

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a fleet is a navy's body of ships

explanation.surface: A naval force on the verge of getting away.
explanation.walkthrough: FLEET loses its last letter to give FLEE.
explanation.definitionFit: To run away from danger is a direct synonym for getting away or breaking free.

clue.text: Boy eating duck in no time at all

indicators.note: whatever eats something takes it inside, so one piece swallows another

blocks.note: a son is a boy
a duck in cricket is a score of nought, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A greedy child wolfing down a duck dinner in record time.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman out for no runs has made a duck, so duck gives the zero-shaped O.
explanation.definitionFit: Shortly or before long means something will happen very quickly, without delay.

indicators.note: something renewed is made over afresh, so the letters are put together in a new form

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the American federal agency will extend the rental on its offices.
explanation.walkthrough: The FBI is the US Federal Bureau of Investigation, but here its three letters are just part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something workable or achievable can be done, so it is a straightforward synonym.

indicators.note: only a small portion of the following words is wanted, a run of letters inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A performer whose acting is somewhat stiff, said with tongue in cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: It is ironic indeed to call one of film's most celebrated actors wooden, which makes the surface a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert De Niro is a famous American film star, so he is an example of a performer.

clue.text: One disposing of wine collection, did you hear?

indicators.note: asks about something heard rather than read, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a wine cellar is a stock of bottles kept by a household

explanation.surface: Gossip about someone getting rid of their stock of fine wines.
explanation.walkthrough: A cellar can mean the stock of wine itself, not just the room; it is pronounced the same as SELLER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who sells goods gets rid of them in exchange for money, so they part with them.

indicators.note: placing one thing within another means it is enclosed by the outer part

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
CE stands for Church of England

explanation.surface: Securing the church plate against thieves.
explanation.walkthrough: CE is the Church of England, the established church in England.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something behind bars is to confine or imprison it, as a verb.

blocks.note: surface reading: a road haulage firm in the north of England
setter's reading: the Arctic animals that pull Santa Claus's sleigh

explanation.surface: A trucking company from the north with an unexpected saintly employer.
explanation.walkthrough: Hauliers sounds like lorry firms; here they are animals hauling a sleigh, and St Nicholas is Santa Claus.
explanation.definitionFit: These Arctic deer, traditionally driven by Father Christmas, drag his sledge across the sky on Christmas Eve.

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A cricket team in which nearly everyone has been dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All but fifteen' reads as a number left over, but 'All but' is the definition; FIFTEEN is spelt out as fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean practically or virtually, as in nearly complete for practical purposes.

blocks.note: first meaning: to delight or enrapture, stressed on the second syllable
second meaning: a foyer or way in to a building

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a pressure group for buses and trains; instead, transport means to carry away with joy.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb sense means to fill someone with delight, while the noun names the hall or doorway where visitors arrive.

clue.text: Criminal alleges ecstasy’s the talk of the bar?

definitions.note: the question mark flags that the bar here is the legal profession

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked or wrong, so the letters are bent out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A crook claims that a drug is the gossip of the local pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The bar looks like a pub, but it is the profession of barristers, who speak in jargon.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the dense technical jargon used by lawyers, collectively known as the bar.

blocks.note: to be at one is to be in agreement
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A parent reconciled with their daughter after a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reunion is apt, since atonement literally means becoming at one again.
explanation.definitionFit: To atone is to make up for a wrong, so the past tense matches compensating for wrongdoing.

clue.text: Check nothing will get you a ban

blocks.note: to vet is to check or examine
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A warning that failing to inspect anything leads to being barred.
explanation.walkthrough: VET plus the zero-shaped O.
explanation.definitionFit: An official prohibition or refusal to allow something is a formal block on it.

clue.text: An old vicar retiring in Italian city

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing or going backwards, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: taken as written
O is the abbreviation for old
Rev is short for Reverend, a vicar's title

explanation.surface: An elderly clergyman spending his retirement in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole string is reversed; 'retiring' reads as giving up work, but signals the turnaround.
explanation.definitionFit: Verona is a city in north-eastern Italy, famous as the setting of Romeo and Juliet.

blocks.note: taken as written
British roads are graded, and the minor class carries the letter B before its number

explanation.surface: A small road found in a foreign country.
explanation.walkthrough: British roads are classed as motorways, A roads (major) and B roads (minor).
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a foreign country, especially across the sea, is the same as being away from home.

clue.text: Express disapproval of bishop? That would be a mistake

blocks.note: to boo is to jeer
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: Jeering at a churchman would be a social blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' just joins the jeer to the bishop; B is a standard abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Boob is British informal slang for a silly blunder or gaffe, an error.

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning upwards makes the letters climb from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
a tad is a small amount

explanation.surface: Uncovering a small piece of intelligence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning up' suggests discovering something, but it signals the reversal in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Facts and figures collected for reference or analysis are a direct synonym for knowledge gathered.

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: a cast or mould is a form
the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A government spokesperson announcing that the actors keep letting everyone down.
explanation.walkthrough: Cast suggests a theatre company, but it is a mould for shaping things.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal and official both describe things done according to recognised rules and procedures, sanctioned by authority.

blocks.note: first meaning: a daily is a British term for a cleaner who comes in each day
second meaning: British slang for a household row, often one the police attend

explanation.walkthrough: Daily looks like an adverb about frequency; in British usage a daily is a cleaner or household servant.
explanation.definitionFit: A household servant is a domestic, and so is a quarrel between partners at home, in British police slang.

clue.text: Husband leaving comfortable position in French city

indicators.note: whatever is leaving departs, so that letter is taken out

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for husband
a niche is a snug, suitable role or place

explanation.surface: A man walking out of a cushy job on the Riviera.
explanation.walkthrough: The husband's H is removed from NICHE.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice is a resort on the Mediterranean coast of southern France, on the Côte d'Azur.
